activism.direction_note: Reconstructed on a comparable scale; the raw Estimate column mixes percent and decimal across studies.

bma.direction_note: Semi-elasticity, not an elasticity: the percentage change in domestic firms' productivity associated with a one-unit (i.e. 0 to 1) increase in the foreign-presence ratio, so a coefficient of 0.1 means a ten-percentage-point rise in foreign presence goes with roughly a 1% increase in domestic productivity. Positive means foreign presence is associated with higher domestic productivity. bma2.pdf states it as 'the semi-elasticity of domestic productivity with respect to foreign presence', and uses the term nine times against no use of a plain elasticity.

border.direction_note: Raw coefficient on the border dummy in a log-linear gravity model; the paper's headline reduction is a transform of it, not the raw value.

dst.direction_note: SIGN TRAP: the stored value is the impact on electricity CONSUMPTION, so NEGATIVE means savings and is the favourable direction (median -0.40). The abstract instead frames the headline as a positive magnitude, 'slight electricity savings: 0.34%'. Taking the sign at face value inverts the finding.

electricity.direction_note: Marshallian-equivalent price elasticity (the paper's Slutsky-converted effect_M), negative by convention. Pools short-, intermediate- and long-run estimates, which the paper analyses separately; condition on the run-length flags in the per-dataset file rather than pooling blind.

esg.direction_note: Points on the Bloomberg/LSEG ESG scale per percentage point of board gender diversity, not a percent change.

euro.direction_note: Raw gravity-model coefficient on the currency-union dummy; the headline trade effect is a transform of it.

forward.direction_note: The null of interest is a slope of 1, not 0. Testing against zero will mislead.

gasoline.direction_note: Long-run income elasticity only; see the dataset note for the short-run estimates. CAUTION on n_obs: it is the file's Observations column, and init.do does weight by sqrt(Observations), but the column counts TIME PERIODS rather than observations. Observations equals Timespan x the data frequency (1, 4, or 12 for annual, quarterly, and monthly) on 100.0% of all 701 rows, exactly, so it carries no cross-sectional dimension at all. That makes it the estimation sample size for a single-series time-series study and an undercount for anything pooled across units. The 90 rows recording 1 are single-year cross sections -- Timespan 1, Start equal to End, Cross_section set on 89 of them -- where the real sample is the number of units and the file never records it. They are NOT a missing-value code, which is what an earlier version of this note supposed. Check Cross_section and the frequency dummies before using n_obs here as a precision instrument.

gasoline_price.direction_note: Negative by convention: demand falls as price rises.

habits.direction_note: Unitless, normally bounded by 0 (no habit) and 1 (full persistence).

house_prices.direction_note: Stored as a PROPORTION: house.do multiplies by 100 for the percentages the paper reports. Negative is the expected direction, higher policy rates lowering house prices. One row per impulse-response horizon, so rows within an IRF are not independent.

incentives.direction_note: Baseline measure. Cohen's d, the paper's robustness variant, is in the per-dataset file.

migrant.direction_note: The stored value is NOT the elasticity. It is the negative inverse: 88.8% of values are negative with median -0.050, and -1/effect has median 15.38, matching the paper's headline substitution elasticity of 13 to about 22. To recover the elasticity take -1/effect, and convert the standard error by the delta method -- se/effect^2 -- rather than using the stored se unchanged. Do NOT pool this column with the other 'elasticity' literatures. Confirmed 2026-08-04 after the Fable and Codex audits both flagged it.

price_puzzle.units: proportional change in the price level
price_puzzle.direction_note: Stored as a PROPORTION, not a percent: multiply by 100 to read as the paper does (median |effect| 0.002 = 0.2%, consistent with its reported 0.33% trough). Positive values are the puzzling price INCREASE after a monetary contraction; theory expects negative. One row per horizon.

reforms.direction_note: Computed here from the reported t-statistic and degrees of freedom, following the paper's own code.

scc.units: US dollars per tonne of carbon

size.direction_note: Raw size-return slopes: NEGATIVE means a larger conventional size premium, i.e. small firms outperforming. The abstract states that researchers prefer estimates showing 'a negative relation between size and returns'. 76% of stored effects are negative. Do not read positive as the premium.

skill.direction_note: The stored `elasticity` column is the substitution elasticity on ALL 1,097 rows. It is not pre-transformed for any of them. What varies is which quantity the paper ANALYSES: skill.do line 16 computes `coefficient = -1/elasticity` from the stored column for every row, then keeps the stored elasticity where `inverted_estimate == 0` (414 rows, 24 studies) and the computed negative inverse where `inverted_estimate == 1` (683 rows, 77 studies, the paper's headline sample of 682). So to reproduce the paper's headline group you apply -1/x yourself; the column does not arrive already inverted. The paper's Table A2 reports each group on its own scale and both reproduce from the published file after the paper's 1/99 winsorisation: the direct group's stored elasticity gives 0.921 against a reported 0.921, and -1/stored on the inverted group gives -0.558 against a reported -0.554. Averaging the stored column across both groups is meaningful only as a statement about elasticities; averaging it as though the two groups were on different scales is not.
skill.direction_note_correction: Corrected 2026-09-05. A note added the previous day said the stored column held 'its negative reciprocal on 683 rows'. That was wrong and it was wrong in the harmful direction: a reader following it would treat the headline rows as already inverted and would not apply -1/x, or would invert twice. If the stored column really were the negative reciprocal on those rows its winsorised mean would be -0.554; it is 4.024. The error was caught by the dataset audit and settled against the paper's own Table A2.

trust.direction_note: Raw size-return slopes: more negative means a larger conventional size premium.

fdi.direction_note: Winsorised FDI spillover elasticity (e_w). No standard error exists in the file, so this dataset supports model averaging over study characteristics but not SE-based synthesis.

lags.direction_note: Transmission lag: months from the monetary shock to the trough of the price response (mon_bot). A duration, not a regression coefficient, so it has no sampling standard error.

substitution.direction_note: Elasticity of intertemporal substitution. Same 2,735 estimates as the eis dataset; this file adds country-level moderators.

spillovers.direction_note: Semi-elasticity, not an elasticity: the percentage change in domestic firms' productivity associated with a one-unit (i.e. 0 to 1) increase in the foreign-presence ratio, so a coefficient of 0.1 means a ten-percentage-point rise in foreign presence goes with roughly a 1% increase in domestic productivity. Positive means foreign presence is associated with higher domestic productivity. spillovers2.pdf Section 2, below Eq. (2): the coefficients 'can be interpreted as semi-elasticities and thus constitute the natural common metric for the economic effect of spillovers'. The paper uses the word semi-elasticity throughout and never calls this quantity an elasticity.
spillovers._note: Units come from overrides.json for this literature; entry added so units.json covers all 39 pooled literatures rather than 38. Absence here previously read as 'no sign trap' when it actually meant 'not present'. Gap found by the Fable audit, 2026-08-04.

finance_growth.direction_note: Positive means financial development is associated with higher growth.
